answer: HYPOTHESIS (proposed submission answer): Within this young-adult NLSY79 cohort (ages 24–32 only), older respondents are less likely to withdraw more money from savings than they put in (DISSAVED): in the full dataset the predicted probability of dissaving falls from ~25–27% at age 24 to ~19% at age 32 (adjusted AGE coefficient −0.049/yr, p<0.001; OR≈0.95), with a mild inverted-U curvature peaking near age 25 (quadratic term p≈0.03–0.05) — a pattern consistent with weaker present bias / greater patience with age within this narrow window. Important caveat: this negative association is not robust — it is driven largely by the ~2,200 respondents whose INCOME/BMI are mean-imputed (savings variables default-imputed to 0; they are older, mean age 29.0), and after excluding them the age effect is no longer statistically significant and its sign flips slightly positive (P age 24 vs 32: 0.264 vs 0.286, p>0.1), so "older = less likely to dissave" should be read as a feature of the supplied file rather than an established life-course time-preference trend.

payload.hypothesis: Within this young-adult NLSY79 cohort (ages 24-32 only), age is negatively associated with the likelihood of withdrawing more money from savings than putting in (DISSAVED): in the full dataset the predicted probability of dissaving falls from about 25-27% at age 24 to about 19% at age 32 (adjusted logistic model DISSAVED ~ AGE + AGE^2 + controls: AGE coef -0.049 per year, p<0.001, OR~0.95; quadratic term negative, p~0.04, mild inverted-U peaking near age 25), a pattern consistent with weaker present bias / greater patience with age within this narrow window. This association is not robust: it is driven largely by the ~2,200 respondents whose INCOME/BMI are mean-imputed (savings variables default-imputed to 0, skewing older), and after excluding them the age effect is no longer statistically significant and its sign flips slightly positive (P dissaving age 24 vs 32: 0.264 vs 0.286, p>0.1), so the negative age effect should be treated as a feature of the supplied file rather than an established life-course time-preference trend.
payload.workflow: 1) Loaded data/nls_bmi_processed.csv (n=12,686, 0 missing); verified AGE_2==AGE^2, binary outcomes, ranges. 2) Data-quality audit: found 2,151 exact-duplicate rows, traced them to 2,200 rows with mean-imputed INCOME/BMI and default-imputed DISSAVED=0 (older, mean age 29.0); 11 implausible BMI>100 rows dropped from models. 3) Centered AGE at 27.86 to resolve corr(AGE,AGE_2)=0.999 (VIF 687 -> ~1.0). 4) Fit logistic regressions DISSAVED ~ AGE_c + AGE_c2, unadjusted and adjusted for GENDER, log1p(INCOME), BMI, BLACK, HISPANIC, on the full file (primary) and on the non-imputed/deduplicated sample (sensitivity); LR tests for the quadratic term; marginal effects and predicted probabilities at ages 24/28/32. 5) Nonparametric shape check with 3 age bins. 6) Secondary exploratory model for SAMESAVE (separate outcome, perfectly nested with DISSAVED, excluded as covariate). 7) Drafted the data-grounded hypothesis with the duplicate/imputation caveat stated explicitly.
